name: 2 - Matching Tools to Purpose Transcript
content:
WEBVTT
 
 Greta Ríos: Thank you so much, Ageda. I will start by saying thank you to everyone who's here, but also thank you to the Allen Lab for Democracy Renovation, to the GOV Lab, and to Innovate US.
 
 Greta Ríos: for having us here. I'm going to speak, like, really quickly about People Powered, and then I'm going to give the mic to my colleague, Michelle, who's going to talk about the important things today. So, what is People Powered, and what am I doing here? As Ageda said, my name is Greta, and I normally work and live in Mexico City. Right now, I am very happy to be in New York at our
 
 Greta Ríos: at our offices in people power.
 
 Greta Ríos: What is People Power? We are a global hub for participatory democracy, and I know that doesn't, that might not ring a bell to many of you, so…
 
 Greta Ríos: What… why People Power, and what is participatory democracy? Well, People Power is an organization that was formed to address the big global challenges to democracy. We addressed two big problems. The first one is that most voices are left out of government decisions.
 
 Greta Ríos: When we… when we talk about democracy.
 
 Greta Ríos: people normally think that we have democracy because we can elect who is going to represent us, but that doesn't mean that we really have opportunities to participate in government decision-making, so we think that we need to create,
 
 Greta Ríos: Ways to make sure that every voice counts, because when people participate in decision making, we have better policies and we have stronger results.
 
 Greta Ríos: But doing this, which in a very technical way is called participatory democracy, is hard.
 
 Greta Ríos: it's hard, and if it's not done correctly, it can be even… even harmful. So, we believe that,
 
 Greta Ríos: democracy, the participatory democracy needs to be done well, and that's why we have a lot of, programs to help advocates do it better. So, in a nutshell, people power expands… exists because we want to expand people's power to make government decisions.
 
 Greta Ríos: by supporting organizations and governments that are building participatory democracy around the world to do it better. So, how we do this is we provide support to these governments
 
 Greta Ríos: For them to be able to enable more participatory democracy. We work, from below. We have a global community of practice that helps us do this, and we have, several, like, tiers of,
 
 Greta Ríos: of involvement that you can… that you can, interact with us, on. We have a lot of communications channels. We are on social media, we create,
 
 Greta Ríos: some resources that are there. We have a resource center with curated resources that can help you understand what participatory democracy is and how to use it. But we also have support programs where we match you with a mentor, or you can take an online course with us and learn how to do this. And most importantly, as I said, we have a community of support, so people powered
 
 Greta Ríos: is a member-based organization. We have members around the world, around 200 members right now, and
 
 Greta Ríos: We… we… we can have organizational members and individual members, so…
 
 Greta Ríos: anyone who is working on participatory democracy, either as a researcher, an advocate, maybe… maybe someone who is actually, you know, in charge of creating participatory programs out there, you can be a people-powered member and meet everyone else in the community and get to our events, and share knowledge, and also share your concerns and find
 
 Greta Ríos: support in the community. So, that's pretty much, what we do, and today Nikhil's gonna talk to you about some of the… of the very concrete work that we have done.
 
 Greta Ríos: in relation to AI and other participatory democracy tools. So, Nikhil, the floor is all yours.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Thank you, Greta.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Hi, everyone. My name is Nikhil Kumar, and I'm based in Brooklyn, and as
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Greta mentioned I'm the resource manager here at People Powered, and my job is really to manage the development of capacity-building resources to support practitioners like you to plan, implement, and improve participatory processes. And I'm excited to talk today specifically about the guidance
 
 Nikhil Kumar: that you need to use digital tools, and specifically those that incorporate AI features in your work.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And I do want to just note, before I get started, that my background is in policy, and when I… when I think about civic tech, I kind of approach it from the perspective of
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Managers in government and civil society who are first focused on supporting good participatory processes that lead to solid policy outcomes.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, for today's session, I really want to approach this topic from… The perspective of…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: helping you to understand what you need to know, what questions you need to ask when dealing with technology in order to support your work, as opposed to really thinking, like, oh, AI is really flashy right now, we need to, like, wedge it into our work.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: I want to focus today on how we can make the technology work for government and civil society.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So… Why are we here today? The purpose of today's session is…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: to introduce you to the guidance you need to select the right AI tool.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: For the right purpose.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And hopefully by the end of today's session, you'll walk away with a framework for matching AI tools to specific goals.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Real examples of AI supporting deliberation, problem solving, and decision making.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: The knowledge and tools that you need to evaluate participation platforms, as well as to spot their limitations.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: the questions to ask before adopting an AI tool, as well as ways to ensure that AI enhances, rather than replacing human judgment.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So today's agenda… we're actually right on schedule, so that's great. We'll have plenty of time, for Q&A after the presentation, but we're gonna start with a quick warm-up.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And I'll… I'll be dividing my presentation into three parts, which, you know, this topic is quite broad, but I think hopefully this is going to be a helpful introduction for you. So I'm going to talk about the challenges and opportunities
 
 Nikhil Kumar: of using AI for participation?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: As well as the specific uses that we see from global practice before, during, and after a participatory process.
 
 Rachel Joan: Fuck!
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And finally, I'll talk about how you can evaluate digital platforms and AI features.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So Let's just start with a quick warm-up. I'd love to do a temperature check in the room.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And, Ageda, could we launch the first poll? Okay, perfect. So, the first question is, have you used digital platforms or tools to support participatory processes before?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And no worries if you're quite new to this.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, and then I see the second one is also there, so…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: I'm also curious if you've used AI features to support participation as well.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, I see some responses coming in.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, I think we can close the poll and display the results.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, so yeah, this is actually very interesting. I'm seeing kind of an even spread.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Between those of you who have done a lot of digital participation, those of you who have a little bit of experience with it.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: As well as those with no experience. And then, on the other hand.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: most people, like, over two-thirds, have not used AI features, or at least you're not aware that you've been using AI features to support participation. Because as we'll see, like, some of them are actually already built into some of the platforms that are used.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, great.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So that was very helpful.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Now I'm gonna share a little bit about the challenges and opportunities of using AI for participation.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And first, just a little bit of background on why we need guidance on digital participation in AI. So.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Based on the poll, as you're… most of you are aware, there are many different digital participation tools out there, ranging from repurposed tools that people already use every day, like common, like, networking apps like WhatsApp or Facebook.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: All the way to comprehensive platforms that have been custom-made to support participatory processes like participatory budgeting, citizens' assemblies, participatory policymaking, and so on.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: In addition, as you're all experiencing on a daily basis in your life and work, AI is increasingly common.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And the participation deliberation space is no exception to this. So many of the platforms that have been used for participation are adopting AI to enhance the experience, both for program hosts and users.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And at the same time, given the number of tools and features out there, and the rapid evolution of the technology, it can be difficult for practitioners in government and civil society to find accessible, relevant, and practical guidance.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So at People Powered, working with our partners and our global community, we've developed a guide to digital participation platforms, which we first released in 2022,
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And this year, actually just last week, we expanded the guidance to include a special section on AI and digital participation. So that's kind of the context of what we're coming to this session with.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: To present to you.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: The guide is for practitioners in governments, other public institutions, civil society organizations, really any practitioner looking to understand the opportunities and challenges
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Related to digital tools and AI, as well as very practical guidance on how to operationalize those tools in your work.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, our process for updating the guide this year was very empirically based.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, we worked with the lead writer, Matt Stempeck, from the Civic Tech Field Guide, as well as partners at UNDP and the Friedrich Nauman Foundation.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And we surveyed platform developers as well as users to understand how people are actually using the tools. So, rather than taking a more theoretical approach to what's possible, we're trying to see what's happening on the ground, because that's probably the most useful for our audience.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And we used a mix of observation, desk research, interviews, workshops, as well as expert review.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And as you can see, the guide is divided into different sections, including an overview of digital participation, a special section on the challenges and opportunities of using AI, guidance for selecting, setting up, and running a digital platform.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Some thoughts for looking ahead, and additional practical resources.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And as I mentioned, we did this work very collaboratively, so…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: we… we worked with our global member community of participatory democracy practitioners, and we also worked with Matt Stempeck from the Civic Tech Field Guide, who brings a wealth of knowledge on the civic Tech landscape.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And specifically related to participation?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: We also worked with the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, based in Taiwan, and with UNDP,
 
 Nikhil Kumar: to really flesh out the details and the case studies of digital participation that uses AI, so that the guide is really reflective of global practice and relevant for different audiences.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: what do we mean by AI? I think AI is a buzzword, obviously, but it's… sometimes it's not really clear exactly what it means, so…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: AI, as we understand it, is really an umbrella term that encompasses an array of different technologies.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And basically, right now, we're calling something AI when it allows a computer to act like a human would. And over time, the technology that we take for granted stops being considered AI. And this is the case, for example, with speech processing.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Over decades of work in speech processing and human-computer interaction, computers have developed to a point where they can decently understand how we talk, at least some of the time if the voices are clear and they're in common languages.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: just to kind of frame the discussion today, when we talk about AI, we're including the full subset of methods, ranging from natural language processing to machine learning.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And, of course, a lot of what's currently referred to AI as generative AI,
 
 Nikhil Kumar: That relies on large language models.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: For the purpose of our session today, we're really thinking about the actual features that each type of AI unlocks, rather than the underlying computer science.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And given how fast-moving and controversial AI is, it's really important, and I really want to emphasize this.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: to approach the issue with a set of principles. So, at People Powered, we developed this year an AI policy to guide our work, together with our community.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And you can see some of the principles that are included in this policy.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Including mission alignment, that the AI is human-centered, that it's transparent.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: That it's accountable, meaning that humans are ultimately responsible for the output and the decisions, even if they use the AI tools.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: In addition, sustainability, equity and inclusion, learning, and of course, privacy and security.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, a lot of these principles are aligned with our organizational values.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And I think that's really important, and I would also encourage all of you to work with the communities that power your work, and the stakeholders that you engage with, to develop your own set of principles to guide your approach, so that it is grounded in your values, and so that you're not just reacting to the latest technology that's being developed.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So… A few of the concerns related to AI I would say that…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: some of the concerns are really kind of the counterpoint of all of these principles, so it's possible that the AI might not be transparent, and, like, it might not be clear how decisions
 
 Nikhil Kumar: arrived at using AI were calculated, or it might not be accountable. As I said, a human might not ultimately be filtering
 
 Nikhil Kumar: the output of the AI,
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, I think, yeah, basically the concerns are that the AI will kind of go against what we value, and then also some specific examples that we've been seeing a lot in research and the media are related to kind of the uncertainty with this new technology. So.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: thinking about what are going to be the economic consequences of the AI? Are there going to be big job losses, including in the governance space?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Will it harm people's critical thinking abilities and possibly even kind of take away the human element of participation?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: I know there's some interesting research now about this, Will the AI hallucinate, plagiarize?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: be sycophantic, There are ways to mitigate this, such as retrieval augmented generation, but
 
 Nikhil Kumar: There are no perfect solutions, of course.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: What is the environmental impact related to water use, energy use, and…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Are the… are the environmental impacts
 
 Nikhil Kumar: equitable. For example, where data centers are cited is often inequitable.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: There might be second-order effects that we don't even know are gonna happen as a result of this new technology.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And then, of course, kind of, like, more philosophically, the potential existential threat to humanity.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Which, maybe the space isn't really the right place to talk about that, but I think it's also helpful to keep that on our minds.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: But yeah, it's not all doom and gloom. We are very excited about the potential for AI to improve participation, both for program managers and participants.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So… One thing that we're seeing on the ground is…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: A boost in efficiency for the running of these processes, which could ultimately lead to more participatory programs, even if
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Participation agencies don't have much budget.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: or staffing, they could use AI to… to help out.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Also, AI is unlocking deeper and new forms of engagement, by bringing in…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: New people who don't often engage in, kind of, innovative methods of engagement.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: it can reduce digital barriers if designed well. For example, if someone isn't comfortable typing, Then they could…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: speak… they could use speech to share their views, and then the AI can… convert that into text.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: more legible inputs from participants. So that's kind of related to
 
 Nikhil Kumar: program managers being able to use AI to
 
 Nikhil Kumar: more quickly and more accurately analyze the inputs, and then also better sense-making of the outcomes of the participatory process, which I'll talk a bit more about.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, so… A quick check-in.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: I'm curious to hear from you guys, what's one challenge that you're concerned about when it comes to AI and participation, as well as one opportunity that you're excited about?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So feel free to type in the chat.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Bias is definitely a challenge.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: That's definitely something to keep in mind.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Privacy. The digital divide, yes.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Ensuring representative samples.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: hallucinations, yep.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Also curious about any opportunities that you guys are excited about.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Replacement for face-to-face, that could be an opportunity or a challenge.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Broader participation, definitely. We see that in the case studies.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Saving time, accessibility.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Summarizing data.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, these are great. Yeah, I think… I'm glad to see that…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: You guys are very interested and informed.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, so…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Now that we have a shared overall understanding of how AI can fit into participatory processes, I'm gonna share some of the specific uses that we're seeing in practice. And as I mentioned, these are based on real-world examples that we found in our research with Matt Stempeck, UNDP, the Global People-Powered Community.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And in the guide, you'll see it can be helpful to think about the uses of AI before, during, and after a participatory process. So that's how I'm gonna break it down here.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: These are some examples.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: That we've seen in practice of…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: program managers using AI before a participatory process to prepare for…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: the actual process. So, that includes streamlining administrative work, which can often be done with general AI tools, like ChatGPT, doesn't have to be
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Like, a specific participatory platform.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Training staff to run the process. Swappable AI models is very interesting. It basically provides for greater flexibility in case a new model is developed that is more appealing, maybe more public service oriented. It could allow
 
 Nikhil Kumar: to swap that new one in. Forming diverse participant groups, which is often relevant for representative processes, like citizens' assemblies and juries.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: As well as simulating participation to test the platform before you get started.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And a couple of… more specific examples…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: We've seen AI being used to plan the process. So, for example, IdeaScale AI provides users with guidance and recommendations to design an innovation campaign, and as you can see in the screenshot, Deliberate also has this feature.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Emporando Juntas from Brazil recommends using AI for this, but doesn't yet offer a feature.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Yeah, as I mentioned, participatory process hosts are also using mainstream models like ChatGPT and Anthropic to brainstorm and develop participatory programs.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And also, we at People Powered are in the process of conceiving an AI tool that can help users to plan participatory processes, so stay tuned for more on that.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Maybe later this year or next year.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Another example of AI before a participatory process is a dynamic FAQ and glossary.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, rather than pre-writing answers to the questions you expect people to have, you can aggregate common questions to your program's chatbot or other AI tool, and publish answers to them. And you can see an example here from PopVox Foundation with their Staff Link tool.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: AI during a participatory process, this is maybe the most exciting slide. Unfortunately, just because of the time limitations, I don't have time to go into all of this, but it's all in the guide, so I definitely invite you to explore that to see everything that's possible.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And I'm gonna share a few screenshots
 
 Nikhil Kumar: of some examples. So, one of the most useful
 
 Nikhil Kumar: uses of AI is parsing, summarizing, and classifying participant contributions.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Compared with traditional survey methods, generative AI's ability to parse large amounts of speech, or text or other forms of engagement
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Can allow hosts to ask more open-ended, qualitative questions.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: That allow people to share how they really feel.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: The AI feature allows administrators to handle large volumes of text, even if they receive 100,000 pages of transcripts, which I'm sure some of you have had to deal with that kind of quantity before. And actually, one note is that AI has been used for years to address this, even before the current gen AI boom.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, more mature participation AI features apply natural language processing to mine large volumes of text and classify discussion topics, or estimate sentiment.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And… They can cluster wide-ranging conversations into a more finite set of topics for participants and process hosts.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Another really common use that we're seeing is transcribing speech, as I mentioned before.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And, yeah, so it's not limited to working with text.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And… The more that platforms allow people to speak as they naturally would, the more accessible the processes become.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And we actually have a case
 
 Nikhil Kumar: that we've written up on our website from Germany's Siegen-Wittgenstein district, where
 
 Nikhil Kumar: urban planners piloted Deliberate, an AI tool, during their participatory social planning conferences, and this used a speech-to-text
 
 Nikhil Kumar: feature, to improve documentation, note-taking, and it also saved the
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Time for facilitators to focus more fully on engaging with participants.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Another common use is assisting participants through the process with bots.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And I want to flag one risk here, is that different participants might have varying experiences with the same support bot, which can lead to unequal treatment.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: For example, a bot might provide two different people a different set of pros and cons about the same proposal, and because of privacy concerns, the process host might not know about these different experiences, so this is something to keep in mind.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Those were just a few examples of AI during a process.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: There are also a few… instances of…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: AI being used after a participatory process, and one of the most interesting is sense-making, which helps participants and admins understand the results of a participatory process. So you can see here that Assemble distills
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Wide-ranging digital debates, and represents them in visually creative formats, like mind maps, videos, even a comic strip summary.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So that's all AI-generated, and it can make communicating about the results of the process
 
 Nikhil Kumar: A lot easier and engaging.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Google's Jigsaw team also launched its own free product, Sensemaker, to provide this service.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And then AI features have also been used to compose written summaries of the process, and to collect and display analytics.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, so another check-in before we get to the final part of the presentation.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: At what stage or stages are you considering using AI to support a participatory process?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, we reached 50% participation in the poll.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, I think we can share the results now.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, this is great.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, there's kind of a plurality for using AI before the process to help prep.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: during the process and after the process, and then… yeah. Okay, so yeah.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: I think, yeah, I think it'll be… it'll be helpful for you guys to all check out the guide, because that provides some very specific
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Examples, as well as advice?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: For how to use these features.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Okay, so now before we go to the Q&A, I want to share a bit of a framework for you to help you evaluate digital platforms and AI features, as well as some resources that can help you with this.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: It's important to take into account what we've spoken about so far, including the challenges and opportunities that AI presents.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: the principles that you want to approach it with, and then the different potential uses of AI features before, during, and after a process.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, when selecting a tool, I think the most important thing to keep in mind, which I mentioned earlier, is
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Think about the tool in service of your participatory process, rather than trying to make your participatory process fit into the shiny new tool.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, what you really need to do is kind of, like, assess and map your goals for the process, both in terms of what you want participants to get out of it, as well as policy outcomes that you want.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Think about your available resources in terms of finances, human resources, technical know-how that you might need to set up and run the digital participation platform or AI feature. And then also, think about your AI principles
 
 Nikhil Kumar: That you want to have in mind before you even think about the tools.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And then, based on that mapping.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: You can kind of identify which needs
 
 Nikhil Kumar: the digital participation tool and the AI feature can mean, both for the end user, which are… which is the participants, and for the host, which is probably you as the program manager.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And then, based on that needs assessment.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: You can identify the tool and the features that are most helpful To meet your needs.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, for example.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Do you need to make the process more efficient from the back end if you have limited human and financial resources to support administrative tasks and data processing?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Or do you need to make the process more accessible for users who speak different languages, in which case you can use translation features, or for those who are less comfortable typing their answers, in which case you can use voice transcription, for example?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And, okay, once you've mapped all of this out, goals, capacities, needs, from the perspective of the user and the host.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: I recommend that you use our ratings of digital participation tools to help you select what's right for your process.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, we have, on our website, we have…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: an analysis of 30 comprehensive tools that have been used to support digital participation globally, and this year we updated the ratings to include more information and insights about each tool. We also made the Airtable, where the ratings are, a bit more interactive, so that you can filter based on your needs.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And then, we also have some special mentions, which are…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: digital tools that are doing a lot to leverage AI.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, this can also be helpful when you're thinking about which tools specifically
 
 Nikhil Kumar: you want to use to harness AI for your process.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And we also worked with Matt Stempeck, as well as our tech review committee on the ratings this year, and we used research insights, expert review, and user and developer surveys.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: The ratings are based on 6 criteria, so you can also kind of think about
 
 Nikhil Kumar: your needs mapped against these criteria. So, the criteria are platform cost.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Capacity requirements, meaning the technical know-how needed to
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Set up and run a participatory platform.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: the different features that are available through the tool. Accessibility in terms of different languages for people with disabilities.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: etc. Ethics and transparency, that includes the data policy, Other security measures… Is the platform open source?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And then track record and reliability. So, how long has the platform been available? How many countries is it used in? How many clients does it have? All these indicators of reliability.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Yeah, so these are some questions to keep in mind when using the ratings. So, is the tool cost-effective, accessible, reliable, and appropriate for your context and program?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: What technical expertise is needed to use it effectively and efficiently?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Does it offer support? Does it offer the features you require? And is it ethical in its data use, protection of personal information, and content moderation?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: We also have these questions that are specific to AI features that you can ask when evaluating the different options.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, think about which AI model the platform relies on, and how that relates back to your AI principles.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: Does the data get shared with the AI provider, the participation platform, a third party? That relates to privacy and security. At which stage of the process is the AI used?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, thinking about… At which stage in the process you would like to use it based on your needs?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: What does the platform use AI to accomplish?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: How will we know it's operating correctly and fairly?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: that relates to transparency. And then, how does the AI perform with the languages spoken by the community?
 
 Nikhil Kumar: because, you know, a lot of AIs are trained on, like, high-resource languages.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: But if there are languages that are less commonly represented in tech, then the AI might not be as useful. So that's something actually quite important to keep in mind.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: And then, before… I… and just to…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: bring us to the Q&A. I do want to share a case study that we researched
 
 Nikhil Kumar: from Northern Ireland about using an AI-powered tool for engagement.
 
 Nikhil Kumar: So, Northern Ireland is, of course, a post-conflict society, and… the… the Voice Matters Initiative
 
 Nikhil Kumar: use… used a digital participation tool provided by Dembrain that harnesses AI to…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: capture speech, and, basically, it allowed… it allowed participants to speak more freely. It also freed up time for facilitators to…
 
 Nikhil Kumar: pay more attention to the work of facilitation, like, in-person facilitation. And, like, all of that kind of built greater trans
 
 [... truncated ...]
